{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q010_rossmann_family_function_divergence","answer":"SCOPe treats these as three distinct families within one homologous superfamily, illustrating functional divergence of a shared ancestral domain. In the current release, SCOPe 2.08, they are:
- Alcohol dehydrogenase-like, C-terminal domain: c.2.1.1, SUNID 51736.
- CoA-binding domain: c.2.1.8, SUNID 51900.
- Potassium channel NAD-binding domain: c.2.1.9, SUNID 63944.

All belong to the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains superfamily, c.2.1 (SUNID 51735). Its homology endpoint explicitly indicates superfamily-level homology. Thus, SCOPe supports probable common ancestry across these families despite potentially weak sequence similarity; their separation into families reflects closer relationships within each group. They also share fold c.2 (SUNID 51734) and class c, Alpha and beta proteins (SUNID 51349). Fold describes shared structural topology, and class describes broad secondary-structure organization; neither level alone establishes common ancestry.

Biologically, a related Rossmann scaffold has been adapted to different ligand-binding and protein contexts: the coenzyme-binding portion of alcohol-dehydrogenase-like proteins, CoA-binding domains, and channel-associated regulatory domains. This domain relationship does not make their complete proteins functionally equivalent. Do not transfer alcohol dehydrogenase activity to the CoA-binding or potassium-channel families, infer CoA binding in the other families, or assume every member binds NAD(P) merely from the superfamily name. Channel-family membership also does not establish a particular gating mechanism or catalytic activity.

A cross-family structure can inform modeling of the conserved domain core, but does not automatically provide a reliable template for ligand specificity, active-site geometry, variable loops, or the complete protein. Functional assignment requires additional evidence: sequence/profile alignments, conserved binding and catalytic residues, ligand-bound structures, domain architecture, and biochemical binding/activity or channel-function measurements. Choose representatives appropriate to the target family and biological context rather than treating one superfamily member as representative of all three functions.","evidence_used":["/api/v1/","/api/v1/openapi.yaml","/api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=alcohol","/api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=CoA-binding","/api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=potassium","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/51735","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/51735/children","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/51735/parents","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/51735/homology"]}]}
